sections.h2: A Chinese menu is a formula, not a list
p: Most dish names are built the same way: **cooking method + main ingredient + cut or flavour**. 红烧牛肉 is red-braised (红烧) beef (牛肉). 清蒸鱼 is plain-steamed (清蒸) fish (鱼). 麻辣豆腐 is numbing-spicy (麻辣) tofu (豆腐).

Learn about forty characters and you stop reading dish names and start reading recipes. You will not know exactly what arrives, but you will know whether it is fried or steamed, whether it is pork or fish, and whether it will hurt.

p: A Chinese menu has hundreds of possible dishes. Chinese signs do not. The same fifty or so words turn up on every metro platform, shop door and toilet corridor from Beijing to Kunming, and most of them are two characters long.

That makes signs the easiest Chinese you will ever read. Learn to recognise 出口 (exit), 禁止 (forbidden) and 洗手间 (toilet) by shape and you are already reading a large share of what is on the walls. The tables below are grouped by where you will meet the words, with Hanyu Pinyin and tone marks so you can say them if you need to ask.

Mainland China uses simplified characters, which is what these tables show. Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan use traditional characters, so 出口 looks the same but 电梯 becomes 電梯 and 厕所 becomes 廁所. Tova reads both.
The first group is the one that gets you out of a building. 口 means mouth, and on a sign it means an opening — a way in or out.

p: Large Chinese metro stations can have a dozen exits spread over several streets. Coming up the wrong one can cost you ten minutes and a road crossing.
ol: **Look up the exit before you arrive.** Map apps and hotel directions usually name an exit letter — "Exit D" or "D口". Write it down.
**Follow 出口 first, then the letter.** On the platform, overhead boards show 出口 with an arrow. Nearer the gates the boards split by letter.

**Read the landmark list under each letter.** Exit boards list the streets, malls and buildings above that exit. This is where the camera earns its place: capture the board and you get every landmark in English with its pinyin, which you can match against the name your hotel sent you.
**Check for 无障碍 if you have luggage.** Not every exit has a lift or escalator. The accessible ones are marked, usually with the wheelchair symbol as well.

sections.h2: A sign you do not understand on a door
p: You reach a door with red characters and no English. Before you push it, look for 禁止 or 请勿 at the start. If either is there, whatever comes next is not allowed.

禁止入内 and 闲人免进 both mean you should not go through. 禁止吸烟 in a stairwell means the stairwell is not the smoking area, however many cigarette ends are on the floor. If the sign is longer than four or five characters, capture it: long signs are often rules or opening hours, and the detail matters.
Shop doors work the same way. 营业时间 followed by numbers is the opening hours, written on a 24-hour clock. 休息 on its own, often hung on a card, means closed for now.

ul: **Reading 出 and 入 the wrong way round.** 出 (chū) is out, 入 (rù) is in. 入 is easy to confuse with 人 (person) — the strokes lean the other way.
**Assuming 酒店 is a bar.** It is a hotel. A bar is usually 酒吧 (jiǔbā).
**Reading a discount as a percentage off.** 七折 means you pay 70% of the price, not that 70% is taken off.
**Trusting the English on the sign.** Many signs carry an English line, and some are machine-translated nonsense. The characters are the reliable part.

**Waiting for a live read on a stylised sign.** Calligraphy, neon and very old shopfronts are hard for any camera. Get closer, tap the shutter for a still capture, and accept that a heavily decorative sign may still come back wrong.

sections.h2: Why your translation app stops working when you land
p: Mainland China filters international internet traffic, and Google's services are on the wrong side of that filter. Google Translate — the app most travellers already have — cannot reach its servers from a Chinese network. Google ran a China-specific version at translate.google.cn for years, but **shut it down in October 2022**, so the old workaround is gone too.

What makes this worse than a normal outage is how it fails. The app opens. The camera turns on. You point it at a menu and nothing happens, or the text freezes half-translated. There is no error telling you the country you are standing in is the problem, so most people assume their phone is broken or the hotel Wi-Fi is slow, and keep retrying at the exact moment they needed an answer.

The fix is not a single app. It is deciding, before you fly, which of your tools work **on the device itself** — with the aeroplane in flight mode, no SIM, no Wi-Fi — because that is the only capability the filter cannot touch. We ran the main apps through exactly that test in [our comparison of the best translator apps for China](/translate/best-translator-app-for-china/).
Tested on an iPhone on a mainland Chinese network in September 2026. Treat it as a starting point rather than gospel: what is reachable changes, sometimes within a single week.

sections.callout: The row that catches people out is Google Translate's. Its **offline packs keep working** even though the app cannot reach the network — but only if you downloaded them before you arrived. Downloading them from inside China is exactly the thing that will not work.

sections.h2: Set it up before you fly
p: Do all of this on your home Wi-Fi. Every step needs a connection that mainland China will not give you. If you are not sure what to download, [the offline translator checklist](/translate/offline-translator-china/) explains the three kinds of offline pack and which ones you need.
ol: **Download offline language packs in every translation app you plan to use.** In Tova, Settings → Offline packs. In Apple Translate, Settings → Translate → Downloaded Languages. In Google Translate, the download arrow next to Chinese.

**Test each one in flight mode before you leave the house.** Turn on aeroplane mode, then actually translate something. An app that shows a spinner in your kitchen will show the same spinner in Chengdu.
**Photograph the things you will need offline** — your hotel booking with the Chinese address, your visa page, the Chinese name of anywhere you plan to go. A screenshot survives a dead network.
**Write down your hotel address in Chinese characters** and keep it on paper. Every taxi conversation starts there, and paper does not run out of battery.
**Install anything you might want later, now.** The App Store itself is reachable in China, but downloads can be slow and some apps are unavailable in the Chinese storefront.

sections.h2: Roaming and eSIMs: the workaround business travellers use
p: If you keep your home SIM active and pay for international roaming, your data is usually routed back through your home carrier's network before it reaches the internet. In practice that means you are browsing as if you were still at home, and the services blocked on local networks often load normally.

The same is true of most travel eSIMs sold for China, which is why they are popular with business travellers. It is not a guarantee — some route locally, and carriers change their arrangements — so check with your provider rather than assuming, and never make roaming your only plan. Roaming data is also expensive enough that camera translation of a long menu is a real cost.
A local Chinese SIM is the opposite: cheap, fast, and filtered exactly like every other domestic connection.

sections.h2: If you are already in China with nothing downloaded
p: Not ideal, but not hopeless.
ul: **Apple Translate is already on your iPhone** and is reachable. It will not give you pinyin, but it will give you meaning.
**The App Store works.** You can still install an app that translates on-device — you just cannot install one that needs Google.
**Hotel Wi-Fi is filtered too.** It is the same internet. A VPN you install after arriving is also likely to be blocked; they have to be set up beforehand.
**Ask.** Staff at any hotel above budget level generally read some English, and pointing at a phone screen works better than you would expect.

sections.h2: Why pinyin matters more than you think
p: Most translation apps give you the meaning and stop. That is enough to order lunch, and not enough to say the name of the dish, ask where the bathroom is, or read the same character again tomorrow and recognise it.

Pinyin — the romanisation above each character — turns a translation into something you can pronounce out loud. In a country where the gap between reading and speaking is the whole problem, that is the difference between pointing at a phone and having a conversation. Tova prints it above every character; Pleco gives it in dictionary lookups; the mainstream translators mostly do not.

The same gap shows up where you least expect it. Chinese stations are named city + direction + 站, so Hangzhou, Hangzhou East and Hangzhou South are three different places and the difference is one character — see [which Chinese train station is on your ticket](/translate/chinese-train-stations/).
Translation is one part of getting ready. For the rest, from entry rules and hotels to payments and mobile data, see our [China travel checklist](/translate/china-travel-checklist/).

sections.h2: Cantonese is not Mandarin with an accent
p: Cantonese is the everyday language of Hong Kong, Macau and much of Guangdong, including Guangzhou. It shares most of its characters with Mandarin, but the sounds are different enough that a Mandarin speaker and a Cantonese speaker cannot follow each other in conversation.

That is the problem with using Hanyu Pinyin in Hong Kong. Pinyin is built for Mandarin. Put pinyin above a Cantonese menu and you get the Mandarin reading of every character, which is not what anyone in the restaurant will say. 飲茶, the word for going out for dim sum, is yǐn chá in Mandarin and jam2 caa4 in Cantonese. Say the first in a Hong Kong teahouse and you will be understood only because the staff guess.

Jyutping is the romanisation the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong designed for Cantonese. It is what Tova uses when you set the language to Cantonese, and it is what the [free Jyutping converter](/tools/jyutping-converter/) on this site produces from any text you paste.
Jyutping marks tone with a number after each syllable rather than an accent over a vowel. Cantonese has six tones, and changing the tone changes the word. The classic set uses the syllable si:
The same characters read in Mandarin pinyin and in Jyutping. None of these are close enough to swap.

p: Written Cantonese uses a handful of characters that standard written Chinese does not, and they are everywhere on Hong Kong menus, shop notices and adverts. A Mandarin-only reader stumbles on every one of them.

ol: **Find the order sheet.** Most dim sum restaurants give you a printed sheet listing every dish, with a box to write the quantity. It is almost entirely characters.

**Capture the whole sheet.** Tap the shutter once and Tova reads the full sheet, with Jyutping above each dish name and the English underneath. For the broader menu vocabulary — cooking methods, proteins, warning words — see [how to read a Chinese menu](/translate/chinese-menu/).
**Mark the boxes, hand it over.** You do not have to say anything. When a trolley or server comes past, 呢個 (ni1 go3, this one) and a point is enough.
**Ask for the bill with 唔該埋單.** m4 goi1 maai4 daan1. A raised hand and a small scribbling gesture works too.

p: Minibuses do not stop at every stop unless someone asks. The route and fare are on a card at the front, usually in characters, so capture it before you get on if you are unsure you have the right one.

When your stop is coming, call out 有落 (jau5 lok6) — getting off — or 前面有落 (cin4 min6 jau5 lok6), getting off ahead. This is the one place where saying it matters more than showing it: the driver is watching the road, not your phone. Practise it with the Jyutping first and tap Listen to hear it.

ul: **Using pinyin in Hong Kong.** It gives you the Mandarin reading. Many people in Hong Kong speak Mandarin, but it is not the language of the street.
**Dropping the tone numbers.** Without them, si could be any of six words. The numbers are the pronunciation, not decoration.
**Mixing up 唔該 and 多謝.** Both mean thank you. 唔該 is for a service — someone holding a door, bringing your food. 多謝 is for a gift or a favour.
**Reading Jyutping as English.** j sounds like English y, so jau5 is close to "yow". c is like ts or ch, so caa4 is close to "chah". eo and oe are vowel sounds with no English equivalent.
**Expecting simplified characters.** Hong Kong and Macau use traditional characters. Guangzhou uses simplified, but the spoken language there is still Cantonese.

The Speak tab shows the Jyutping for what was said. If you lose signal, translation falls back to on-device translation and Jyutping is still shown.

Written Cantonese is less standardised than Mandarin, and colloquial spellings vary between signs. Some slang and very new words will get a literal or odd translation. The Jyutping for common characters is dependable; treat the translation of heavily colloquial text as a guide.

p: Pinyin is the romanisation that turns 你好 into nǐ hǎo. The marks over the vowels are tones, and they change the word rather than decorating it: mā is mother, mǎ is horse, mà is to scold.

Travellers routinely decide tones are a refinement to worry about later. They are not — they are part of the word, in the way that swapping a vowel would be in English. Getting them approximately right is what makes the difference between being understood and being smiled at.
You will get them wrong. Say it anyway; people correct you, and the correction is how you learn.

p: Written Japanese uses three scripts at once, often in the same word. Romaji — Japanese written in the Latin alphabet — is the fourth, and it exists mostly for people who cannot read the other three yet. Knowing which script you are looking at tells you a lot before you know what any of it says.

Hiragana and katakana are syllable alphabets of 46 basic characters each: every character is one sound, and the sound never changes. Kanji are the characters borrowed from Chinese, and each has a meaning and usually several readings. A sentence like 駅で水を買います (eki de mizu o kaimasu, I buy water at the station) switches between kanji and hiragana four times.

sections.h2: The romaji rules that trip people up
p: Signs, maps and rail networks in Japan use Hepburn romaji, the system built for English speakers. It is mostly spelled the way it sounds, with a handful of rules that catch everyone out.

head: Japanese
Romaji
The rule
rows: A long vowel is marked with a line, ō. Signs often drop it and write Tokyo; you may also see Toukyou
おお is also a long o
In katakana the dash ー lengthens the vowel before it
A small っ doubles the next consonant — hold it for a beat
Before ch the doubling is written tch
ん is n. Traditional Hepburn writes m before b, m and p, so you will also see shimbun
An apostrophe separates ん from a following vowel: cause
The particle は is read wa, not ha
The particle へ is read e, not he — to the station
The particle を is read o — water, as the object
し ち つ ふ じ
Hepburn spells these as they sound to English ears

sections.callout: Japanese schools also teach a second system, Kunrei-shiki, which writes the same sounds as si, ti, tu and hu — so 富士 can appear as Huzi instead of Fuji. You will rarely see it on signs, but it explains the odd spelling in older textbooks.

p: This is the part that makes kanji hard, and the reason a simple lookup table cannot give you romaji. Most kanji have a Chinese-derived reading (on'yomi), used mainly in compound words, and a native Japanese reading (kun'yomi), used mainly when the character stands alone or takes a hiragana ending. Some have more than one of each, and place names follow their own rules.
The right reading depends on the word the kanji sits in. The table shows how far apart they get.

It also means romaji is a good guess, not a guarantee. Personal names and some place names have readings that even native speakers check. For a station, the romaji on the platform sign is the authority; for a person's name, ask them.

**Tap to hear it.** Listen before you say it. Japanese gives every syllable roughly the same length, so Shinjuku is shin-ju-ku, not SHIN-jook.

ol: **Look for katakana first.** Many product names are loanwords. Sound out the katakana and you often recognise the English word underneath — サンドイッチ is sandoitchi, sandwich.
**Then the kanji.** Flavours and ingredients are usually kanji: 鶏 for chicken, 豚 for pork. Scan the label if you need the detail.
**Check the dates.** 賞味期限 (shōmi kigen) is best before; 消費期限 (shōhi kigen) is use by.

ul: **Reading romaji as English.** Vowels are always a, i, u, e, o, as in Spanish or Italian. Sake is sa-ke, not sayk. Karaoke is ka-ra-o-ke.
**Dropping long vowels.** They change the word. おばさん obasan is aunt; おばあさん obāsan is grandmother.
**Ignoring the small っ.** 来て kite means come; 切手 kitte means postage stamp.
**Over-pronouncing u.** In desu and masu the u is usually barely heard: dess, mass.
**Reading は as ha everywhere.** It is ha inside a word and wa as a particle. こんにちは ends in wa.
**Expecting one reading per kanji.** 生 alone has at least five common readings. If a romaji dictionary gives you one reading for a character, it is not the whole story.

p: Big stations in Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto have English on the main signs, and first-time visitors are often surprised how far that gets them. The trouble starts one layer down: the paper notice taped to a closed exit, the fare adjustment machine, the shop door that says it is shut today, the bus stop in a small town, the warning on a hiking trail.

Those signs use a small, repetitive vocabulary. The same forty or fifty words cover most of what you will meet, and many of them are two kanji long. Learn to recognise the shapes in the tables below and you can usually tell an exit from an entrance before your phone is out of your pocket.
If the scripts are new to you, [reading Japanese with romaji](/translate/read-japanese-romaji/) covers hiragana, katakana and kanji, and the spelling rules that make romaji look odd.

p: Transfers are where most people get lost, because a line can change operator, colour and name at the same station.
ol: **Follow 乗り換え, not 出口.** Transfer signs keep you inside the gates. Following an exit sign by mistake puts you outside, and in some stations that means paying again.
**Match the line colour and letter.** Tokyo Metro and Toei lines each have a colour and a letter, and every station has a number, like G09. Those appear on the signs even where the English does not.
**Read 方面 on the platform.** Each platform names the end of the line or a big stop the train is heading towards. Check it against your map app before you board.
**Check the train type.** A 快速 or 特急 can run straight through your station. If yours is small, a 各駅停車 is the safe choice.

**Scan the notice board if something is wrong.** Delays and suspensions often go up in Japanese first. Tap the shutter on the board, then pinch to zoom into the part you need and translate just that region — it is far more reliable than reading a whole crowded board in one go.
**Choose the exit before you leave the platform.** Large stations have dozens of exits, numbered like A1 and B7 or named by direction, and they can be ten minutes' walk apart above ground.
**Get the exit from your map app.** Most walking directions name a station exit. Look for that number or 東口, 西口 and so on in yellow signs above the platform.
**Check the neighbourhood map by the gates.** It shows which exit leads to which street. Scan it if the landmark names are only in Japanese.
**If you exit wrong, go back through the gates.** In many stations that is quicker than walking round the outside.

p: Convenience stores are easy to use without Japanese, but the staff will ask a few quick questions at the till.
ol: **温めますか** (atatamemasu ka) — do you want it heated? Nod for a bento, shake your head for a sandwich.
**袋はご利用ですか** (fukuro wa goriyō desu ka) — do you need a bag? Bags cost a few yen. はい (hai) for yes, 大丈夫です (daijōbu desu) for no thanks.
**ポイントカード** (pointo kādo) — do you have a points card? いいえ (iie), no, is the answer.
**Check 消費期限 on anything fresh.** Dates are usually written year, month, day.

ul: **Mixing up 入口 and 出口.** Both end in 口, mouth or opening. 入 goes in, 出 goes out. The first kanji is the whole difference.
**Reading 準備中 as open.** A shop with its lights on and a sign saying junbichū is not ready for customers yet.
**Missing 定休日.** Many restaurants close one fixed day a week. The door sign names the day, and it is easy to walk past it and wait.
**Taking a 特急 on a regular ticket.** Limited expresses often need a surcharge ticket. The conductor will ask for it.
**Assuming English means complete.** English signs cover the main route. Closures, detours and temporary notices are frequently Japanese only.
**Pointing the camera at a whole board from across the concourse.** Get closer, or capture it and zoom in. Small text at a distance is where every camera translator, Tova included, gets things wrong.

p: A translation tells you a sign says Shimokitazawa. The romaji tells you how to say it to a station attendant, and it matches the name the train announcer uses. That matters when you are listening for your stop, not reading it.

Tova shows the romaji above each character in a panel at the bottom of the camera screen, with the English underneath, and you can tap to hear it. Kanji readings need a connection, because the same character is read differently in different names. Offline, Tova still translates the sign on your phone, but the romaji may not appear. Save your station and hotel address while you have signal. If Korea is next on the trip, [translating Korean signs](/translate/korean-signs/) works the same way, with Revised Romanization.

faqs.a: Open Tova, set the camera scan language to Japanese, point at the sign and tap the shutter. You get the English meaning and romaji above each character, so you can also say the place name aloud when you ask for directions.

faqs.q: Does it work on the small print on station boards?
faqs.a: Zoom in first. After you take the shot you can pinch to magnify the photo and translate only the part you are looking at, which is far more reliable than trying to read a whole crowded board at once.

faqs.a: 改札, kaisatsu, is the line of ticket gates. 出口, deguchi, is the exit from the station to the street. You pass the 改札 first, then follow signs to the numbered 出口 you want.

h1: Translate a conversation between three languages
lede: Two-way translation covers a taxi. It falls apart the moment a third language joins the table. Boardroom mode keeps three languages on one phone, and you pass the floor from speaker to speaker with a tap.
steps: Turn on Boardroom mode in Settings (a Pro feature), then open the Speak tab.
Set the two main languages, then tap + 3rd in the chip row and choose the third speaker's language.
Before each person talks, tap the swap arrow until their language is highlighted, then tap the mic.

p: Most translator apps are built for two people: you and a waiter, you and a taxi driver. Put a third language at the table — a supplier who speaks Mandarin, a colleague who speaks Japanese, and you in English — and one of you ends up waiting while the other two talk, or someone is drafted in as an interpreter and stops taking part.

Boardroom mode is Tova's answer. It is part of Tova Pro. One phone sits in the middle of the table, holding three languages, and the person holding the floor is whoever you have selected. Each turn is transcribed with its reading, translated, and can be played aloud with Listen.

It is worth being clear about what it is not. It does not listen to the room and work out who is talking. You tell it, with a tap, every time the speaker changes. That sounds like a chore and in practice becomes a rhythm within a few turns — the same rhythm as passing a microphone.

The Speak tab has a row of language chips across the top. With Boardroom on, the row reads: first language, the swap arrow, second language, and a **+ 3rd** chip. Tap + 3rd and pick the third language; that chip then shows the language name, and the third speaker becomes the active one so they can start straight away.

The swap arrow cycles the floor: first speaker, second speaker, third speaker, back to the first. The highlighted chip is the language Tova is listening for. Speech recognition only works in one language at a time, which is why getting the highlight right matters more than anything else in this mode.

Each time you tap the mic, Tova listens for one utterance and stops when the speaker pauses. Tap it again for the next turn. To drop the third speaker, tap the cross on the Boardroom banner and the conversation goes back to two languages.

sections.h3: A supplier meeting with an agent in the room
ol: **Set the languages before anyone sits down.** For example English, Mandarin, and a third language for a colleague. Do a two-line test so everyone sees what happens on the screen.
**Put the phone flat in the middle, screen up.** People read the translation as well as hear it, and numbers are far easier to check on screen than by ear.
**Make one person responsible for the swap arrow.** Usually whoever called the meeting. Everyone else just talks when the highlight is on their language.
**Keep turns to one or two sentences.** Long turns produce long transcripts where a single misheard number hides in the middle. Short turns are easier to correct.
**Confirm prices, quantities and dates in writing afterwards.** Treat the conversation as the negotiation and an email as the record.

ol: **Choose the languages people actually speak at home.** If grandparents speak Cantonese rather than Mandarin, pick Cantonese — the transcript comes back with Jyutping, which the [Cantonese guide](/translate/cantonese-jyutping/) explains.
**Let whoever holds the phone run the swap arrow.** Nobody else needs to touch it.
**Use Listen for anyone who does not want to read a screen.** The translation is spoken aloud, which suits older relatives better than small text.

ol: **Set the guide's language plus the two languages in your group.**
**Ask the guide to pause between points.** The mic stops when the speaker stops, so natural pauses are what split the talk into turns.
**Save the useful answers.** Place names and directions can go to Favourites, which keeps the reading so you can show it later.

ul: **Forgetting to pass the floor.** If the second speaker talks while the first speaker's language is still highlighted, Tova listens in the wrong language and the transcript comes back as nonsense. Tap the arrow first, every time.
**Expecting automatic speaker detection.** Boardroom mode does not detect who is talking. Someone has to select the speaker.

**Assuming every turn is translated for everyone.** Each turn produces one translation. Do a short test exchange first and check which language each speaker's turns come out in, so the person who most needs to follow is not left out.
**A language the phone cannot listen in.** Speech recognition depends on iOS. If Tova says it cannot listen in a language, adding that language's keyboard in iOS Settings usually fixes it.
**Using it for anything legally binding.** Machine translation is good enough to hold a conversation. It is not a certified interpreter, and a contract needs one.

sections.h2: When a human interpreter is still the right call
p: For a first meeting, a site visit or a dinner, Boardroom mode keeps everyone in the conversation without a fourth person at the table. For a signing, a dispute, a medical appointment or anything where one mistranslated word costs real money, pay for an interpreter.

If you are travelling in mainland China, the rest of your translation set-up matters as much as the meeting itself — the [comparison of translator apps for China](/translate/best-translator-app-for-china/) covers which ones keep working without a VPN.

faqs.a: No. You tap the swap arrow to choose the speaker before they talk, and it cycles through the first, second and third language in turn. Speech recognition listens in one language at a time, so the selected speaker has to be the one talking.

faqs.q: Who is three-way translation for?
faqs.a: Mixed-language meetings, family dinners across generations and group travel with a local guide — any situation where two-way translation forces someone at the table to sit out.

faqs.a: Yes. Cantonese is a separate language in Tova from Mandarin, and Cantonese transcripts come back with Jyutping readings rather than pinyin.

p: We built Tova for one specific gap: reading signs, menus and labels in a script you cannot pronounce, in a country where the obvious app does not work. Since our September test it has also moved into the places where the rest of a China trip happens: the chat with your host, and the Chinese apps you order food and rides in. Both are in the next section.

Also new: a Lock Screen button that opens the camera in one tap (iPhone, iOS 18), an Apple Watch app (Pro), Common Replies, which show the answers you are likely to hear back (Pro), and Explain this menu, which says what each dish usually is and which allergens to ask about (Pro). Where another app is still better: **Pleco is a deeper dictionary**, with a decade of lexicography, stroke order and flashcards. **DeepL translates long documents better.** **Apple Translate is free and already installed** if the gist is all you need. **Use it if** you want one app that reads, speaks, replies in WeChat and translates Chinese apps, with the pinyin to say it. **Skip it if** you only need the gist and already have an app that gives you one.

sections.h2: New: translating inside WeChat and Chinese apps

Each app was installed on an iPhone, given its offline packs on home Wi-Fi, then used on a mainland Chinese mobile network and on hotel Wi-Fi in September 2026. h1: Tova vs Google Translate in China
lede: Google Translate is one of the best translators in the world, and in mainland China most of it switches off. Here is what still works, what travellers complain about, and where Tova fits — including the parts where Google is still the better app.

p: **Inside mainland China, Google Translate only works offline.** Google discontinued the service there in 2022 and its servers are filtered, so anything that needs a connection fails. The offline language packs keep working, because they run on your phone — if you downloaded them before you arrived.

**Tova reaches its own servers from inside China without a VPN**, and falls back to on-device translation when there is no signal at all. It also prints pinyin above every character, which Google does not do. And it works where the trip actually happens: its keyboard writes your WeChat replies, and screen translate reads Chinese apps such as Meituan. Google's versions of both need its servers.
**Everywhere else, Google is the more complete app.** It covers more languages, its camera translates in place over the image, and it costs nothing with no ads.
sections.callout: Reachability tested on a mainland Chinese mobile network and hotel Wi-Fi in **September 2026**. What is filtered in China can change without notice. Check before you rely on it.

p: We read the one- and two-star App Store reviews of Google Translate in four English-speaking storefronts. Most are about interface changes anywhere in the world. Three themes matter for a China trip.
ul: **It stops translating in China.** “I went on a trip to China and doesn't translate anything,” a UK reviewer wrote in November 2025. That is the expected result of the 2022 shutdown, but many visitors only discover it at the airport.

**Offline mode is not always there when you need it.** This is the most repeated recent complaint: languages that will not download, packs that vanish or must re-download after an app update, and “downloaded” languages that still ask for a connection. Anywhere else that is an annoyance. In China it is the whole plan, because a missing pack cannot be fetched once you are inside.

**Pronunciation is an afterthought.** Reviewers complain that pinyin is cut to one line on long sentences, that tone marks are too small to tell ì from í, and that offline Japanese shows no romaji under the kanji. If you want to say the words, not just understand them, this is the gap.

p: **Outside China, and for breadth.** Google lists up to 249 languages to Tova's 118, and it has been refined for nearly two decades. For French, Spanish or German it is the stronger choice.

**The camera overlay.** Google translates on top of the image, so the English sits where the Chinese was. Tova reads the text into a panel below the camera with the readings stacked above each character. Ours is better for learning how to say the words; Google's is quicker for getting the gist of a crowded street.
**Free with no ads.** Google Translate has no ads and no paid tier. Tova's free tier shows ads.

**If you prepare.** Download Chinese for offline use on home Wi-Fi, check it in aeroplane mode, and Google gives you a usable offline translator in China. [Our offline translator guide](/translate/offline-translator-china/) explains what an offline pack does and does not cover.

sections.h2: Where Tova is the better fit in China
p: **It keeps working when you are online.** Tova's translation runs through our own backend, which is reachable from mainland China without a VPN, so you get full online translation instead of the cut-down offline mode. When the network drops, it falls back to translating on the phone.

**You can say what you read.** Every character on a scanned sign or menu gets its pinyin printed above it, the way the [Chinese signs guide](/translate/chinese-signs/) shows. Cantonese gets Jyutping and Japanese gets romaji, rather than Mandarin pinyin on a Hong Kong menu.
**The offline path keeps the pinyin.** When Tova falls back to on-device translation for Chinese, the result still carries pinyin above each character.

**It works where you actually talk to people.** Most conversations in China happen in WeChat. Google's translate-as-you-type lives in Gboard on Android and needs Google's servers, so it does nothing there. Tova Keyboard works in WeChat and every other app, on iPhone and Android, with the pinyin and a back-translation so you can check what you are sending. [How Tova Keyboard works](/keyboard/).

**It reads the Chinese apps you need.** Food delivery, restaurant reviews and shopping happen in Meituan, Dianping and Taobao. Tova's screen translate floats a small window over them and shows what the screen says in your language. Google's on-screen translation is Android only and Lens needs Google's servers.

**It is one app for all of it.** Camera with pinyin, two- and three-way voice, the WeChat keyboard and screen translate share the same languages and readings, and all of them work from inside mainland China.

sections.h2: Getting either one ready before you fly
p: The same rule applies to both apps: anything you need from the internet, get it at home.
ol: **Install the app at home.** On Android both apps come from Google Play, which is blocked in mainland China.
**Download offline languages on home Wi-Fi.** For Google, Chinese in the app's offline settings. For Tova, the offline packs in Settings, plus the on-device translation languages your phone offers.
**Test in aeroplane mode.** Translate a sentence and scan a photo of a menu. An app that stalls in your kitchen will stall in Chengdu.
**Keep a second app.** Apple Translate works in China on an iPhone, and Pleco is fully offline for single words.

p: China reachability comes from our September 2026 test on a mainland Chinese mobile network and hotel Wi-Fi, described in [the best translator app for China](/translate/best-translator-app-for-china/). Google's features and language count were checked against its App Store listing and help pages on 8 November 2026. The complaints come from Google Translate's one- and two-star App Store reviews in the US, UK, Canadian and Australian stores; we used only themes that repeat, and left out complaints Google has since fixed, such as the missing Cantonese it added in 2024.

By default Tova uses Google's translation engine on its servers, so this page is not a claim that our translations are better than Google's. The difference in China is whether you can reach them. You can check that yourself with the aeroplane-mode test in [our China no-VPN guide](/translate/china-no-vpn/).

title: Chinese Train Stations — Which One Is On Your Ticket
metaDesc: Hangzhou, Hangzhou East and Hangzhou South are three stations, one character apart. How to read 东 南 西 北 on a ticket, and why your passport is part of it.
keywords: chinese train station names, hangzhou east station, beijing west vs beijing south, shanghai hongqiao station, which train station china, china high speed rail passport
h1: Which Chinese train station is on your ticket?
lede: Most Chinese cities have three or four main stations and the English names differ by one word. Get it wrong and you are across town from a train you cannot rebook. The whole distinction is four characters.
steps: Find the station characters on your ticket or booking — they are next to the city name.
Check the last character before 站: 东 is East, 南 South, 西 West, 北 North.
Put that station into your map app in Chinese, not English, and check the travel time from where you are staying.

sections.h2: The mistake is one character wide
p: 杭州站, 杭州东站 and 杭州南站 are three separate stations in Hangzhou, several kilometres apart. In English they come out as Hangzhou, Hangzhou East and Hangzhou South — close enough that a tired traveller books one and turns up at another.

Chinese station names are built the same way every time: **city + direction + 站**. 站 (zhàn) means station. The character in front of it is the whole difference, and there are only four of them worth memorising.

This matters more than it sounds, because the fast trains usually do not leave from the station named plainly after the city. The plain one is often the old central station handling slower services; the high-speed lines were built later, on the edge of town, and got a direction in the name.

sections.callout: **上海虹桥 (Shanghai Hongqiao) shares its name with the airport**, and the station and terminal sit next to each other on the same metro stop. That is convenient if you are connecting and confusing if you are not — check whether your ticket says 虹桥站 or 虹桥机场.

sections.h2: Wuhan, where the stations do not say Wuhan
p: Every rule above assumes the station name contains the city name. Wuhan breaks it. Its three main stations are 武汉站, 汉口站 and 武昌站 — and two of those do not contain 武汉 at all.

Hankou (汉口) and Wuchang (武昌) are old districts of the city that kept their own names, so an English itinerary reading "Hankou" gives no clue that you are in Wuhan. Travellers have stood in the wrong one.
Other cities do this on a smaller scale. If a station name looks nothing like the city you booked, that is normal — look it up rather than assuming the booking is wrong.

sections.h2: Your passport is part of the ticket
p: Chinese rail runs on a real-name system, 实名制 (shímíngzhì). The ticket is tied to the passport used to buy it, and the passport has to be with you: you show it to enter the station, again at the gate, and it can be checked on board.

Practically that means the passport number goes in at booking, the name must match the passport exactly, and whoever travels has to be the person on the ticket. You cannot hand a spare ticket to a friend.

Foreign passports usually cannot use the automatic gates that residents tap through with an ID card. Look for the staffed lane at the end of the gate line — it is normal, it is quick, and it is the one that catches people who queued in the wrong place.

sections.h2: Reading the station on the day
p: Signage inside is consistent nationwide, so the same handful of characters gets you from the door to the platform.

head: Sign
Pinyin
What it is
rows: Waiting hall — where you sit until boarding

ol: **Read the station in Chinese, not English.** The Chinese name is unambiguous; the English one is a transliteration that loses the direction if you skim.
**Search your map app with the Chinese characters.** Typing "Hangzhou station" can return any of three. Pasting 杭州东站 returns exactly one.
**Check the travel time from your hotel.** These stations are often 40 minutes apart, and the fast one is usually the far one.
**Confirm the passport name matches.** A middle name that is on the passport but not on the booking is a real problem at the gate, not a formality.
**Photograph the ticket.** You will want the 车次 train number and the 检票口 gate number when the departure board is a wall of characters and you have four minutes.

p: A translation app that gives you "Hangzhou East Railway Station" has technically answered, and you still cannot match it against the departure board, because the board says 杭州东站 and you are scanning for letters.

What helps is seeing the characters with the reading above them, so 东 stops being a shape and becomes dōng, East — something you can recognise at a glance on a ticket, a board, and a platform sign. Four characters is a very small thing to learn for how much it prevents.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Hangzhou and Hangzhou East station?
faqs.a: They are two different stations several kilometres apart. 杭州站 is the older central station; 杭州东站 (East) is the larger high-speed hub and is where most fast trains to Shanghai and Beijing leave from. Check which one your ticket names before you set off.

faqs.q: Which Shanghai station do high-speed trains use?
faqs.a: 上海虹桥站, Shanghai Hongqiao, handles most high-speed services. It sits beside Hongqiao Airport on the same metro stop, so confirm whether your ticket says the station (虹桥站) or the airport (虹桥机场).

faqs.q: Do I need my passport to take a train in China?
faqs.a: Yes. Chinese rail uses a real-name system: the ticket is tied to the passport it was booked with, and you show that passport to enter the station and again at the gate. The name on the booking has to match the passport exactly.

faqs.q: Why is the station called Hankou and not Wuhan?
faqs.a: Hankou (汉口) is a district of Wuhan that kept its own name, as did Wuchang (武昌). Wuhan has three main stations and only one of them, 武汉站, contains the city name. It is normal, not a booking error.

faqs.q: How do I tell which station a Chinese sign means?
faqs.a: Read the character immediately before 站: 东 is East, 南 South, 西 West, 北 North. A name with no direction character is usually the older central station. Scanning a sign or ticket with Tova prints the reading above each character so the direction is readable at a glance.

title: China Travel Checklist: 10 Things to Sort Before You Go
metaDesc: Ten things to sort before a trip to mainland China: entry rules, flights, hotels, mobile data, payments, trains, sights, airport arrival and language.

h1: China travel checklist: 10 things to sort before you go
lede: Ten things to sort out before a trip to mainland China, in roughly the order you’ll need them. None of it is difficult, but several steps are far easier at home than after you land.
disclosure: Some links on this page go to Trip.com, which pays us a small commission if you book. It doesn’t change your price, and we only link to things we’d use ourselves.

p: Whether you need a visa, and which kind, depends on the passport you hold, how long you’re staying and how you’re arriving. Visa-free entry and visa-free transit arrangements exist for some passports, and the lists change often, so treat anything you read on a travel blog, this page included, as a prompt to check rather than as the answer.

Two sources are worth your time: your own government’s travel advice for China, and the Chinese embassy or consulate that covers where you live. While you’re there, check how much validity and how many blank pages your passport needs.
ul: **Government travel advice:** [United States](https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/international-travel/International-Travel-Country-Information-Pages/China.html), [United Kingdom](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/china), [Canada](https://travel.gc.ca/destinations/china), [Australia](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/asia/china), [New Zealand](https://www.safetravel.govt.nz/destinations/china), [Ireland](https://www.ireland.ie/en/dfa/overseas-travel/advice/china/)
**Embassies:** [Chinese embassies, listed by country](https://www.fmprc.gov.cn/eng/zwjg/zgdsg/), from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
**Entry and transit policies in English:** [National Immigration Administration of China](https://en.nia.gov.cn/)

p: If you can, arrive in one of the major hubs such as Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou or Chengdu. More airlines fly there, and onward trains and domestic flights leave all day, so a delay costs you an hour or two and not a night.

If you’re seeing more than one region, price up flying into one city and home from another. It often costs about the same as a return and saves a day of doubling back. Book in your name exactly as it appears in your passport.
sections.soft: We usually check Trip.com for this. [Here’s a good place to start comparing flights](aff:flights).

sections.h2: Choose hotels that accept foreign guests
p: Not every hotel in mainland China is set up to host foreign guests. Hotels have to register each foreign guest’s passport with the local police at check-in, and some smaller and budget places don’t, so travellers still report being turned away at the desk, sometimes late at night with a paid booking in hand.

The simplest way to avoid a surprise is to book through an international platform that shows whether a property takes guests from outside mainland China, and to keep the confirmation where you can find it. A few other things are worth doing while you choose:
ul: Pick somewhere a short walk from a metro station. It makes the first couple of days much easier.
Save the hotel’s name and address in Chinese characters as a screenshot, so you can show it to a driver without a signal.
Have your actual passport with you at check-in. A photo of it won’t do.
If you’re staying with friends or in a private flat, ask your host how registering your stay with the local police works. Hotels do it for you; private stays don’t.
sections.soft: We usually book our own China hotels through Trip.com. [Here’s a good place to start](aff:hotels).

sections.h2: Sort out mobile data before you land
p: Maps, payments and your translator all need a connection, so it helps to have one from the moment you leave the plane. An eSIM is the easy route: you buy it online, install it at home by scanning a QR code, and it switches on when you arrive.

Check first that your phone supports eSIM and isn’t locked to your home network. Many travel eSIMs also keep apps like Google Maps working as they do at home; our guide to [translating in China without a VPN](/translate/china-no-vpn/) explains what does and doesn’t work once you’re there.
sections.soft: We usually check Trip.com for this too. [Here’s the China eSIM we’d look at first](aff:esim).

p: Mainland China is largely cashless. Street stalls, taxis and corner shops all expect you to scan a QR code, and some small places struggle to make change for notes.

Alipay and WeChat Pay both let visitors link many foreign bank cards. Install them at home, where you can still receive the verification text on your usual number, add a card, and finish the identity check with your passport. Make sure the card shows as active before you fly, and carry a little cash in yuan as a backup.

High-speed rail is the best way to travel between most big cities: fast, punctual and comfortable, and you see the country on the way. Tickets are tied to your passport, so book with the number of the passport you’ll be carrying and bring it to the station, where staff check it at the gate. The official railway site, [12306](https://www.12306.cn/en/index.html), has an English version.

Seats on popular routes sell out around public holidays such as Chinese New Year and the National Day week, so book as soon as sales open for your dates. Big cities have several stations with near-identical names; our guide to [Chinese train stations](/translate/chinese-train-stations/) shows how to tell which one is on your ticket.
sections.soft: We usually check Trip.com for this. [Here’s a good place to start looking at trains](aff:trains).

p: Many of the best-known sights, the Forbidden City among them, limit daily visitors and need a reservation made in advance under your real name and passport number. Popular days go quickly, so decide which places matter most to you and book those first.
Bring the same passport you booked with, because it’s your ticket at the gate. And check each site’s closing day before you fix your plan, since many museums shut one day a week.
Our guide to the [top 10 places to visit in China](/translate/top-places-to-visit-china/) covers how each of the big ones is booked, and which days they close.
sections.soft: Where a site’s own booking page is hard to use from abroad, we usually check Trip.com. [Here’s a good place to start with attractions and tours](aff:attractions).

p: You’ll land tired, possibly before your payment apps have been tried in a real shop, and the taxi queue is a poor place to find out. A pre-booked transfer means the driver already has your hotel’s address and the fare is already paid.

If you’d rather make your own way, the big airports have a metro or airport express line into town, and official taxis leave from the marked rank. Either way, have your hotel’s address in Chinese ready to show.
sections.soft: We usually check Trip.com for this. [Here’s a good place to start looking at airport transfers](aff:transfers).

p: Outside major hotels and airports, expect very little English. Menus, street signs, ticket machines and most drivers work in Chinese only. Two small habits cover most situations: keep your hotel’s name and address in Chinese characters as a screenshot you can show without a signal, and download a translator that works offline while you’re still on home Wi-Fi.

We make one ourselves. Tova Translate reads signs and menus through your camera and shows the pinyin above the characters, so you can say a dish or a station name out loud. It’s free on the [App Store](app:ios) and [Google Play](app:android). For the detail, see our guides to [setting up an offline translator for China](/translate/offline-translator-china/) and [reading a Chinese menu](/translate/chinese-menu/).
Run through this a day or two before you leave. Ticks are remembered on this device, and the button prints just the list.

sections.h2: Apps to have ready before you go
p: Install these at home and sign in to each one before you fly. Several send a code by text message to verify your phone number, and on Android, Google Play can’t be reached from mainland China, so anything you forget is hard to add later.

apps.name: Alipay
apps.text: The easiest way to pay with a foreign card. Its built-in mini-programs also cover taxis and metro rides in many cities.

apps.name: WeChat
apps.text: China’s messaging app, and how hotels, hosts and drivers will usually contact you. WeChat Pay works as a second way to pay.

apps.name: Amap
apps.text: The map most people in China use, with public transport and walking directions. Google Maps is blocked, and on an iPhone, Apple Maps works too.

apps.name: DiDi
apps.text: China’s main ride-hailing app. Get the China version, or book a DiDi from inside Alipay without installing anything.

apps.name: Trip.com
apps.text: Trains, hotels, flights and attraction tickets in English, paid with a foreign card. [Get Trip.com](aff:apps).

apps.name: Tova Translate
apps.text: Our own app. It reads signs and menus through your camera with the pinyin above each character, keeps translating when you lose signal, and its keyboard translates what you type in WeChat. Free on the [App Store](app:ios) and [Google Play](app:android).

faqs.q: Do I need a visa to visit mainland China?
faqs.a: It depends on your passport, how long you are staying and how you arrive. Visa-free entry and visa-free transit arrangements exist for some passports and they change often, so check your own government’s travel advice and the Chinese embassy or consulate for your country before you book.

faqs.q: Can foreigners stay at any hotel in China?
faqs.a: Not always. Hotels register foreign guests’ passports with the local police, and some smaller places are not set up to do it, so travellers are occasionally turned away at check-in. Booking through an international platform that shows which hotels accept foreign guests avoids the surprise.

faqs.q: Do I need an eSIM for China?
faqs.a: You do not need one, but it is the easiest way to be online the moment you land. A travel eSIM installs by QR code before you fly and switches on when you arrive, and many keep apps like Google Maps working. Check first that your phone supports eSIM and is not locked to your home network.

faqs.q: Can I use Alipay or WeChat Pay with a foreign bank card?
faqs.a: Yes. Both apps let visitors link many foreign bank cards. Set them up at home, where you can still receive the verification text on your usual number, check the card shows as active before you fly, and carry a little cash as a backup.

h1: How to order food in China as a foreigner
lede: In many restaurants in China the menu is a QR code on the table: you scan it with WeChat or Alipay, order on your own phone and pay in the same screen. Here is how that works for a visitor, what to do when it asks for a Chinese phone number, and how to read a menu that is only in Chinese.
query: order food in China as a foreigner
steps: Scan the QR code on the table with Alipay or WeChat, then screenshot the menu that opens.
In Tova’s Camera tab, pick the screenshot from your photos: each line comes back in English with pinyin above every character.
Go back to the menu and tap the dishes you chose, or point at them for the waiter and read the name out using the pinyin.

faqs.q: How do you order food in China if you don’t speak Chinese?
faqs.a: Many restaurants put a QR code on the table: scan it with Alipay or WeChat, pick dishes from the menu that opens, and pay in the same screen. Where there is no code, point at a picture menu or at a dish on another table. To read a menu that is only in Chinese, screenshot it and open the screenshot in a translator such as Tova, which shows the English and the pinyin for each line.

faqs.q: Can I order from a QR code without a Chinese phone number?
faqs.a: Often, yes: the menu opens inside Alipay or WeChat, and foreigners can open mobile payment in China with an overseas phone number. Some restaurants also ask you to share your phone number or follow their WeChat account before you can order. If you get stuck at that step, ask for a paper menu, order at the counter, or ask the staff to order for you.

faqs.q: Can foreigners pay with Alipay or WeChat Pay?
faqs.a: Yes. Both let visitors link foreign bank cards, including Visa and Mastercard. Set them up before you fly, while you can still receive verification texts on your usual number, and carry some cash as a backup: China’s central bank has said it will act against merchants who refuse cash.

faqs.q: Does Tova work in China without a VPN?
faqs.a: Yes. When Tova cannot reach a server it translates on your phone instead, so the camera and the pinyin keep working with no VPN and no signal. Set up offline translation on home Wi-Fi before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the menu explainer free?
faqs.a: Reading a menu with the camera, in English with pinyin, is free. Explain this menu, which describes each dish and the allergens it commonly contains, is part of Tova Pro. It is a guide, not a safety check: always confirm allergies with the staff.

p: Ordering in China works in one of three ways, sometimes all in the same restaurant: a **QR code on the table** that opens the menu on your phone, a **paper or picture menu**, or a **counter** where you point and pay. QR ordering usually runs inside WeChat or Alipay as a mini-program, a small app that opens inside the big one, so there is nothing extra to install ([Sixth Tone](https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1007222)).

You can do all of it as a visitor. Alipay and WeChat Pay accept foreign bank cards, and foreigners can open mobile payment in China with an overseas phone number ([People’s Daily, published by the People’s Bank of China](https://www.pbc.gov.cn/en/3688006/5275451/5275458/2025080817515864625/index.html)). When a QR menu gets stuck, ask for a paper menu or order at the counter, and keep some cash: the central bank’s stated line is “no refusal to accept cash” ([People’s Bank of China briefing, March 2024](https://www.pbc.gov.cn/en/3688241/3688663/3688666/2025080817504215799/index.html)).
The rest of this page goes through each step, the phone-number problem, paying, and how to read a menu you cannot read.

ol: **Find the code.** It is usually on a stand or a sticker on the table, sometimes with a table number beside it.
**Scan it from inside Alipay or WeChat,** with the app’s own Scan button. The restaurant’s menu opens inside the app, usually with a photo of each dish.
**Add dishes to the basket,** then check it before you confirm.
**Pay in the same screen,** with the card linked to the app. The order is placed without you having to flag anyone down.

sections.h2: When it asks for a phone number or to follow an account
p: Not every restaurant stops at the menu. When reporters looked at 72 restaurants with scan-to-order in 2021, 35 made customers follow the restaurant’s WeChat account first, and 20 asked for access to the phone number linked to the customer’s WeChat account ([Sixth Tone](https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1007222)). In 2023 a Shanghai chain was reported to have no paper menus at all, with a membership sign-up as the only way to order ([China Daily](https://global.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202306/14/WS6489ce46a31033ad3f7bc421.html)).

Regulators have pushed back: the same China Daily report says Shanghai’s market regulator fined a catering company 50,000 yuan in 2021 for collecting customers’ personal information through QR-code ordering. You will still meet these screens. If one stops you, there are other ways in:
ul: **Ask for a paper menu.** Some places keep one for customers who ask.
**Order at the counter,** or wave someone over and point.
**Ask the staff to order for you.** China Daily found coffee-shop staff placing orders on their own phones for customers who would not use the app.

p: Show these on screen or try saying them; the pinyin is there so you can.

head: Say this
Pinyin
Meaning
rows: Do you have a paper menu?
I don’t have a Chinese phone number
kěyǐ bāng wǒ diǎn cài ma

p: Alipay and WeChat Pay both let foreign users link international cards, including Visa and Mastercard ([gov.cn, April 2024](https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202404/11/content_WS6617c858c6d0868f4e8e5f4d.html)). Set them up at home, where you can still receive the verification text on your usual number, and check with your bank that the card works abroad. The [China travel checklist](/translate/china-travel-checklist/) covers the setup step by step.

In 2024 the People’s Bank of China raised the single-transaction limit for overseas visitors using mobile payment from US$1,000 to US$5,000, which covers any normal restaurant bill ([PBOC briefing](https://www.pbc.gov.cn/en/3688241/3688663/3688666/2025080817504215799/index.html)).

Cards and cash still work in many places. A card is accepted where its network’s logo is shown at the till, UnionPay cards are accepted at every merchant terminal ([gov.cn](https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202404/11/content_WS6617c858c6d0868f4e8e5f4d.html)), and the central bank has said it will act against merchants who refuse cash. Carry a little in yuan for the times the app does not cooperate.

Alipay has added translation into 16 languages for some of its services, such as ride-hailing and hotel booking ([People’s Daily](https://www.pbc.gov.cn/en/3688006/5275451/5275458/2025080817515864625/index.html)). A restaurant’s own menu page inside it may still be only in Chinese, which is where the next section comes in.

sections.h2: Reading a QR menu you cannot read
p: A QR menu is Chinese text on your own screen, so you cannot easily point a camera at it. Screenshot it instead.
ol: **Screenshot the menu** inside WeChat or Alipay. If it is long, scroll and take a few.
**Open Tova, go to the Camera tab and pick the screenshot from your photos.** Each line comes back in English, with Hanyu Pinyin above every character.
**Zoom in on one part.** Pinch to zoom on a section and tap **Translate this view**, or use **Crop & Translate** to pick out a single dish.
**Go back and order.** Match the characters on the menu to the ones in your translation; the first two characters of a dish name are usually enough to find it.

p: A paper menu is quicker still: point the camera at it and tap the shutter, and the whole page comes back at once. In the live camera view, each line Tova reads has a button that shows it in large type, to hold up for the waiter. The pinyin means you can also say the dish out loud, which helps when the waiter comes to check. For the forty-odd characters that do most of the work on any menu, see [how to read a Chinese menu](/translate/chinese-menu/).

sections.h2: When the signal drops, or Google is blocked
p: Google’s services are blocked in mainland China, so Google Translate cannot reach its servers there without a VPN. Tova keeps translating when it cannot reach a server: the translation runs on your phone, and the pinyin is still there. Set this up on home Wi-Fi before you fly; the [offline translator guide](/translate/offline-translator-china/) shows what to download, and [translating in China without a VPN](/translate/china-no-vpn/) explains what does and does not work once you are there.

Tova Pro adds **Explain this menu**. After a capture that looks like a menu, it goes through the dishes one by one: what each one is, how it is usually made, the allergens it commonly contains and how spicy it tends to be. Pro can also show any translation full screen and flip it to face the person across the table.
Treat the explainer as a first look, not a safety check. It describes how a dish is usually made, kitchens differ, and it can miss an ingredient.
sections.callout: **Do not rely on a phone for a severe allergy.** Machine translation drops negations and kitchens cross-contaminate. If a reaction would put you in hospital, carry a card written by a native speaker, show it, and ask the staff.

h1: China for gamers: esports hotels, arenas and anime shops
lede: China has more esports hotels than any other country, a pro league with home arenas in five cities, and whole malls given over to anime figures and game goods. Here is how to plan a trip around them as a foreign visitor, including the parts that still need a Chinese ID.
disclosure: Some links on this page go to Trip.com, which pays us a small commission if you book. It doesn’t change your price, and we only link to things we’d use ourselves.

p: An esports hotel (电竞酒店, diànjìng jiǔdiàn) is a hotel whose rooms come with gaming PCs, high-refresh monitors and proper chairs, often two to five machines in one room so a group can play together. There are more than 20,000 of them in China. Some are small independent places, others are rooms set aside inside ordinary chain hotels.

Most of the ones you can book in English take foreign guests. On 20 November 2026 we opened every hotel on Trip.com’s esports pages for the nine cities below, 348 listings in all, and all but two said guests from all countries and regions are welcome. The exceptions are real, though: some esports hotels on the site only take mainland Chinese ID cards. Each hotel page has a **Guests Accepted** line, and the city lists don’t show it, so open the hotel and read it before you pay.
Most dedicated esports hotels are adults only: 50 of the 56 we checked require the guest checking in to be 18 or over.

**Beijing:** [esports hotels in Beijing](aff:gEsportsBeijing)

sections.h2: Know where the pro teams play
p: China’s League of Legends league, the LPL, gives several teams a home arena in their own city. The rest play at the league’s venue in Shanghai. For the 2026 season the home arenas were:

ul: **Honor of Kings (KPL):** teams are tied to cities too, among them AG Super Play in Chengdu, eStarPro in Wuhan, TTG in Guangzhou and Wolves in Chongqing. The finals move to a different city every year: the 2025 final filled the Bird’s Nest in Beijing with 62,196 people.
**Teams move between seasons.** Check the schedule on lpl.qq.com, or the KPL’s own announcements, before you book a city around a match.

p: The main Chinese teams in each game with a league or major events in China, with the city they play from where it is known. Pick a game, then tap a team for a recent result and its official account.
A few arenas keep coming back for the biggest events, and they are worth a visit even on a day with nothing on.
**Mercedes-Benz Arena, Shanghai** (梅赛德斯-奔驰文化中心) hosted Dota 2’s The International in 2019 and still holds esports finals and concerts. [Hotels near Mercedes-Benz Arena](aff:gNearMercedes).

**Beijing National Stadium, the Bird’s Nest** (国家体育场, 鸟巢) held the League of Legends World Championship final in 2017 and the KPL annual final in 2025. [Hotels around the Olympic park](aff:gNearBirdsNest).

**Hangzhou Esports Center** (杭州电竞中心), in Gongshu district, was built for esports at the 2022 Asian Games (held in 2023) and kept as an esports venue afterwards. [Esports hotels in Hangzhou](aff:gEsportsHangzhou).

LPL tickets are sold only on two Chinese ticket apps, **Piaoxingqiu** (票星球) and **Maoyan** (猫眼), and through their WeChat mini programs. The official site and the league’s WeChat account send you there.

Every ticket is bound to one person’s ID, and the league’s 2026 notice says overseas fans may use a foreign passport. You can buy at most two tickets per match, the name is checked against your ID at the gate, and tickets can’t be changed once bought. Payment is through WeChat Pay or Alipay, so set one of them up with your foreign card before you try. Commentary in the arena is in Chinese.
For KPL matches, the notices we read asked for an ID card and did not mention passports. Ask the seller before you buy, or buy through a ticket agent who has done it before.
sections.callout: Big finals sell out in minutes. Have the ticket app installed, your passport added as a real-name ID and WeChat Pay or Alipay working before sales open.

p: Big international events held in mainland China and Hong Kong, by genre. We only list events whose organiser has announced the city; where only a month or a window is known, it says so. League seasons such as the LPL and KPL are not listed one match at a time: the LPL usually starts in mid-January, and both leagues publish their schedules on their own sites.

**Chinese game accounts** use real-name registration tied to Chinese ID. Whether a foreign passport works depends on the game, so don’t count on making a new account for a Chinese server while you’re there.

title: Korea for Gamers: PC Bangs, LoL Park and Game Shops

h1: Korea for gamers: PC bangs, LoL Park and game shops
lede: Korea plays its games in PC bangs, watches them at LoL Park, and hosts the League of Legends World Championship again in 2027. Here is how to do all of it as a visitor, without a Korean phone number.
disclosure: Some links on this page go to Trip.com, which pays us a small commission if you book. It doesn’t change your price, and we only link to things we’d use ourselves.

p: A PC bang (PC방) is Korea’s version of a gaming café: rows of fast PCs with good chairs and headsets, often open around the clock, with food you order from the screen and staff bring to your seat. They are everywhere, and they are where most Koreans play.

You don’t need a Korean phone number. At the kiosk, choose **non-member** (비회원), pay by cash or card, and take the number it gives you. Find a free seat on the seat map and type the number in to log on. Membership gets lower rates and keeps unused time, but it needs Korean phone verification. Smoking is banned in PC bangs.
Prices vary by place and time of day. The team-branded PC bangs below cost more than a neighbourhood one, and come with merchandise, lounges and food.
sections.callout: No non-member button on the kiosk? Show the counter this: 비회원으로 이용할게요 (“I’ll use it as a non-member”).

sections.h3: PC bangs run by pro teams
ul: **T1 Base Camp Gangnam**, two minutes from Sinnonhyeon Station: a 24-hour PC zone, the T1 flagship store and a trophy room. [Hotels near Sinnonhyeon](aff:kNearSinnonhyeon).
**Gen.G GGX** in Dongdaemun: 252 PCs and a Gen.G store with items sold only here.
**RedForce PC bang** in Jonggak, about 200 seats, linked underground to LoL Park.
**T1 Base Camp Busan** in Haeundae: a PC café, T1 Shop and esports pub.

p: Unlike China, Korea has no big esports-hotel scene. Trip.com has esports pages for Seoul and Busan, but when we checked them on 20 November 2026 most listings were ordinary hotels; only a handful listed a gaming computer or gaming chair in their facilities.

If you want a room with a gaming PC, look for “Gaming computer” in the facilities and check the room photos before you book. Otherwise stay near a PC bang; they are easy to find in any busy neighbourhood.
ul: **Seoul:** [esports hotels in Seoul](aff:kEsportsSeoul)
**Busan:** [esports hotels in Busan](aff:kEsportsBusan)

sections.h2: Watch the LCK at LoL Park
p: LoL Park (롤파크) is the home of the LCK, Korea’s League of Legends league. All ten teams play here, in an arena of about 450 seats that wraps around the stage, so you sit a few metres from the players. It is on the third floor of Gran Seoul at 33 Jong-ro, Jonggak Station Exit 1, with a Riot Store, a PC café and a café in the same space.

Overseas fans buy tickets on **NOL World** (world.nol.com), in English. Korean residents use NOL Ticket. Big matches, especially T1’s, sell out in seconds, so be logged in and ready when sales open. Bring your passport to the match.
[Hotels near LoL Park](aff:kNearJonggak) put you a short walk from Jonggak Station.
**KSPO Dome** (올림픽체조경기장) in Olympic Park held the 2026 LCK finals. [Hotels near KSPO Dome](aff:kNearKSPO).
**BEXCO** (벡스코) in Busan hosts G-STAR, Korea’s biggest game show, every November, and held the 2026 Overwatch Asia finals during the show. [Hotels near BEXCO](aff:kNearBEXCO).
**KINTEX** (킨텍스) in Goyang, north-west of Seoul, hosts AGF and PlayX4, and has held StarCraft finals. [Hotels near KINTEX](aff:kNearKINTEX).

**Worlds 2027** comes to Korea: the quarterfinals and semifinals at Suwon Convention Center (수원컨벤션센터), and the final at Seoul Arena (서울아레나), a new arena being built in Chang-dong. [Hotels in Suwon](aff:kHotelsSuwon).
Events in Korea where the organiser has named the city. Where only a window or a month is known, it says so. LCK matches run most of the year at LoL Park; the 2027 schedule is not out yet.

title: Top 10 Places to Visit in China (and How to Book Them)
metaDesc: Zhangjiajie, the Great Wall, the Forbidden City, the Terracotta Army and six more, with a map, how foreigners book each one, when to go and the signs you’ll see.

h1: Top 10 places to visit in China, and how to book them
lede: Five landscapes and five pieces of history, from the sandstone pillars of Zhangjiajie to the painted caves of Dunhuang. For each one: where it is, how a foreign visitor books it, how long to give it and the Chinese you’ll see at the gate, with a map, a booking table and the best season for every place.
disclosure: Some links on this page go to Trip.com, which pays us a small commission if you book. It doesn’t change your price. Trip.com is a reseller, not the official seller: where a site sells its own tickets, we link its official channel first.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit in China for a first trip?
faqs.a: The Great Wall and the Forbidden City in Beijing, the Terracotta Army in Xi’an, the Li River at Guilin and Yangshuo, and Zhangjiajie’s sandstone pillars are the five most people put first. All five link up by high-speed train, so they make a two-week route.

faqs.q: Can foreigners book Forbidden City tickets?
faqs.a: Yes. The Palace Museum’s official website has an English version where you book with your passport. Tickets go on sale seven days ahead, nothing is sold at the gate, and the museum is closed on Mondays except national holidays. Bring the same passport and enter at the Meridian Gate.

faqs.q: How many days do you need in Zhangjiajie?
faqs.a: Two to three days for the core Wulingyuan park, with a night in Wulingyuan town at the park gate. Add a day each for Tianmen Mountain and the Grand Canyon glass bridge, which are separate parks with their own tickets.

faqs.q: Is the Tianmen Mountain cable car running?
faqs.a: Not the long one from the city. It stopped carrying passengers in October 2026, and no reopening date had been announced in November 2026. Visitors were going up by a shorter cableway to Tianmen Cave and then escalators through the mountain. Check the park’s official notices before you go.

faqs.q: Do I need to book Chinese attractions in advance?
faqs.a: For most of the big ones, yes. The Forbidden City, the Terracotta Army, Jiuzhaigou and the Mogao Caves all need a booking made in advance under your passport, and there is a daily limit on visitors. The Great Wall at Mutianyu and Badaling and the lake at Hangzhou are exceptions.

faqs.q: When is the worst time to visit China’s famous sights?
faqs.a: The National Day holiday from 1 to 7 October, the May Day holiday at the start of May and the Spring Festival holiday. Most of China travels then, trains sell out and many sites reach their daily limit.

p: We chose these for a first or second trip: places a traveller can reach without a tour, that look like nothing else in the country, and that are worth the journey even if you only have a week. The table is in the order of the page; the routes further down put them in the order you’d travel.

sections.h2: Zhangjiajie: the stone pillars of Wulingyuan
p: Thousands of sandstone pillars, some over two hundred metres tall, rise out of forest in north-west Hunan. The park inside the Wulingyuan Scenic Area is the one most visitors mean by Zhangjiajie, and one of its pillars was renamed after the film Avatar, whose floating mountains it resembles. Eco-buses run between the trailheads, and the Bailong Elevator and the Tianzi Mountain cableway lift you onto the ridges for an extra fare.

The park ticket covers several days, which is how the park is meant to be seen: stay in Wulingyuan town at the gate rather than in Zhangjiajie city, and go out early before the tour groups arrive. Fog is common and can close in a view for hours, so a spare day helps.

Tianmen Mountain and the Grand Canyon glass bridge are separate parks with their own tickets. The long cableway up Tianmen Mountain from the city stopped carrying passengers in October 2026; in November 2026 visitors were going up by a shorter cableway to Tianmen Cave and escalators through the mountain, so check the park’s notices before you plan around it.

facts: Ahead in busy seasons, through the park’s official mini program. Ticket windows at the gates have staff who help in English.
High-speed train to Zhangjiajie West, then about an hour by road to Wulingyuan town.
Two to three days, plus a day each for Tianmen Mountain and the glass bridge.
High: steep stone steps and long walks between viewpoints. The elevator and cableways save the climbs.
April to June and September to early November.

sections.h2: The Great Wall at Mutianyu, Badaling or Jinshanling
p: The stretches north of Beijing are the Ming dynasty wall most people picture, running along ridges for as far as you can see. Which section you choose matters more than anything else about the day.

Mutianyu is restored, wooded and less crowded than Badaling, with a cable car, a chairlift and a toboggan down. Badaling is the most visited section and the easiest to reach, with its own station on the high-speed line from Beijing to Zhangjiakou. Jinshanling, across the border in Hebei, is partly unrestored and much quieter; it’s a long day from the city and the best of the three for walking. Simatai is entered through Gubei Water Town and is known for evening visits.

According to the Beijing government’s visitor pages, Mutianyu and Badaling don’t need a booking and sell tickets on site; Badaling has English-speaking ticket windows and machines that take foreign cards. Go early, and avoid weekends and holidays at Badaling.

Badaling by high-speed train from Beijing Qinghe; Mutianyu and Jinshanling by road.
A full day including the journey.
Medium to high: the wall is steep in places. A cable car does the climb at Mutianyu.
April to May and September to October.

sections.h2: The Forbidden City and the Temple of Heaven, Beijing
p: The palace of the Ming and Qing emperors is the largest collection of old wooden buildings in China, a walk of courtyard after courtyard from the Meridian Gate in the south to the Gate of Divine Might in the north. The Temple of Heaven, a short metro ride south, is where the emperors prayed for good harvests; its round blue-roofed hall is one of the best-known buildings in the country, and the park around it fills with people exercising and singing in the early morning.

The Palace Museum sells tickets only in advance. Sales open at 20:00 Beijing time seven days ahead on its official website, which has an English version where you book with your passport and an email address; nothing is sold on the day, and weekends and holidays go fast. Enter at the Meridian Gate with the same passport. If the booking won’t go through, the museum’s help line, 400-950-1925, answers in English. The Temple of Heaven books one to seven days ahead through its official WeChat account, and sells at the ticket office on the day if it isn’t full; the Beijing government says no third-party seller is authorised for it.

sections.h2: The Terracotta Army and the city wall, Xi’an
p: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers, each with its own face, were buried around 210 BC to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China. Pit 1, the size of an aircraft hangar, is the one in the photographs; pits 2 and 3 and the bronze chariots in the museum are worth the extra hour.

The museum is in Lintong, about 40 km east of central Xi’an. Every visitor needs a real-name booking with a timed entry, made on the museum’s official website or its WeChat channels, and a passport is accepted. Many sellers resell tickets and tours, so check that you’re buying the official ticket or a tour that includes it.
Back in the city, the Ming city wall is complete all the way round. Hire a bike on top and ride the 13.7 km loop, ideally late in the afternoon.
